subject: physics
title: Acceleration
summary: Acceleration is how quickly velocity changes — speeding up, slowing down, or turning is all acceleration. A launch-up bike that climbs from 0 to 10 m/s in 5 s accelerates at 2 m/s every second. Explore a pedal-driven cart this time, and watch acceleration bend a velocity-time graph upward or downward.

plainLanguageExplanation: Acceleration is the meter of change — how fast velocity changes every second. If a car rolls from rest to 20 m/s in 5 seconds, its acceleration = (20 − 0) / 5 = 4 m/s²: every single second, it's gaining 4 m/s of speed. The s² in the unit is why: it's 'velocity gained, per second.' Acceleration isn't only about going faster. A brake pad slowing a train ( −3 m/s²) is still acceleration — in reverse. So is running a curve while keeping speed: velocity turns, and turning is a change of velocity. It comes from motion only when a net force shows up (Newton's second law). The model lets you drive a cart and trace the velocity line on a screen, bending it steeper when you push the gas and dipping it negative when you brake.
whyItMatters: Acceleration is what actually connects force to motion — the formula a = (final speed − initial speed) ÷ time is the doorway to Newton's second law and to understanding everything from rocket launch to the jolt of a sudden stop. It also explains car 'g-force', why brakes need power, the weight you feel in an elevator, and the push-back in your seat when a bus starts. Kids feel acceleration on every playground swing and every bike jump, and physics finally names it.
didYouKnow: 'G-force' in sports cars and rides isn't a force you feel — it's acceleration, how rapidly your velocity changes, expressed in units of Earth's gravity. A top rocket can yank its crew through big numbers of g at liftoff.
compareReason: Velocity asks how fast you are going and which way; acceleration asks how quickly that velocity is changing — pairing them on one cart reveals the layering.
